en: [Kāmandakī]: [1] “From birth” (*ājanma*). Those specific actions of yours that have been delightful for even a moment since birth—now that they are remembered, they cause us pain both internally and externally; and those same charming and sweet flatteries do likewise. (XX) They “burn the body,” which refers to external suffering; “the heart,” which refers to mental suffering. [B78b] [1] [2] “Unstable” (*aniyata*) means fickle. “Incoherent” (*asamañjasa*) means having a disconnected meaning. [2]

MADAYANTIKĀ and LAVAṄGIKĀ: Alas, dear friend, you whose face is as beautiful as a radiant moon, where have you gone? What sudden turn of ill fortune has befallen you, who are so delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, while you were all alone? Noble Mādhava, the world of the living has become for you one in which the great festival has set.

[Kāmandakī] [3] That in which there is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) called *śṛṅgāra* characterized by fresh passion; "one who has performed the auspicious rites" (*kṛtakautuka*): one upon whom various auspicious substances have been bound, as they say: "The grass called *bhadrā*, white mustard, peacock feathers, snake skins, bracelets, and medicinal herbs—these are proclaimed as the items known as *kautuka*. (1) *Bhadrā* refers to white *guggulu*. In the interpretation of *lavalī* and *lavaṅga*, it means "fresh," "passion" (*rāga*) meaning redness, and "flavor" (*rasa*) meaning that which produces moisture. *Kautuka*: wonder. *Niyati*: destiny.
A collection of winds: a whirlwind (*vātyā*). [3]
Lavaṅgikā: O hopeless one, your heart is made of adamant; you are utterly cruel.
Madayantikā: Friend Lavaṅgikā, am I not saying this? Please, take heart for even a single moment.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, what can I do? My life does not leave me, as if it were fixed and immovable by a firm cement of adamant.
[Kāmandakī] "Ujjihānam": emerging.

[4] Regarding the heroine (*nāyikā*): she is one whose "ālokau" (two lights) are "ujjvalau" (brilliant), that is, whose eyes are clear; she is "snigdhā," meaning affectionate. "Malīmasam" means lusterless. Regarding the flame of a lamp (*pradīpaśikhā*): "ālokaḥ" is light. "Snigdhā" means smeared with oil and the like. "Malīmasam" means blackened by being burnt. [4] "Praguṇīkṛtāni" means made abundant or brought to perfection.

[5] *Stanyanyāsaḥ*: the cessation of suckling at the breast. *Dantapañcālikā*: a doll made of ivory. Since this is so, I have been your benefactress from childhood onwards. Nevertheless, she shook her head with an interrogative intonation of reproach, as if to say: "Even so, you do not show me greater affection than you do toward your own mother. (2) [5]

[6] *Akāraṇam*: that which has an unknown cause. *Smeram*: a smile. That in which there is such a smile is "a smile without cause" (*akāraṇasmeram*). For this very reason they say: "A smile without cause, adorned with a black *tilaka* mark—those devoid of merit do not behold the lovely face of the charming one, O charming girl. The alternative reading of the Kashmiris, *ākāraṇam āhvānam* ("without cause" means "calling out"), is an interpretation that does not follow the traditional transmission (*asāṃpradāyika*). Placing white mustard seeds on the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and the forehead is for protection. *Stanaṃdhayaḥ*: one who drinks from the breast; a suckling infant. [6]

Lavaṅgikā: O Blessed One, be gracious! I am no longer capable of sustaining this life through such a reckless act. (4) Casting myself down from this king of mountains, I shall find peace. Therefore, may the Blessed One grant me such a blessing that I may behold my dear friend even in another birth.
(*Avadhūya*: having cast down).

[Kāmandakī] [7] But how can the abandonment of life due to separation be justified if it results in reunion? Furthermore, reunion is not inevitable for living beings subject to diverse karmas. As it has been said: "Even a dead man is unable to follow his own deceased [kinsmen]; for, with the exception of one's wife, the path to Yama diverges for everyone. (5) Therefore, she says: "Reunion.
[Lavaṅgikā] — Just as you command.
[Madayantikā] — What do you command? That I should go ahead? I am attentive.
Lāvaṅgikā: Friend, be gracious; desist from this attempt at suicide. Do not forget that person.
(6) Madayantikā: Begone! I am not subject to your will—that is to say, I am not dependent on you.

MADAYANTIKĀ: My lord Makaranda, homage to you! LAVAṄGIKĀ: Blessed lady, this is indeed that mountain peak where the sacred girdle is bound by the stream of the Madhumatī river. "Madhumatī" is the name of the river. "Saṃdānita" means bound. "Pavitra" means pure or holy. "Viṭaṅka" means a high, projecting point.

[Behind the scenes] [9] Regarding worldly objects such as sovereignty and the like. *Suvarṇabindu*: The Blessed Lord, the husband of Bhavānī, who is purifying at the confluence of the Madhumatī and Sindhu rivers.
[9] MADAYANTIKĀ and LAVAṄGIKĀ: Suddenly, the auspicious sight of Mālatī and Mādhava has occurred. (XX) "Suddenly" means a great calamity.
*Atyāhita*: A great danger, or an action that disregards one's very life. (7)

[Kāmandakī and Makaranda] [10] *Āsāra*: A shower of those trees whose leaves are swords; that is to say, a downpour of sword-blade-leaves. Due to hearing the unpleasant news concerning Bhūrivasu, it is a shower of sword-leaves (*asipattrāsāra*); due to the confirmation of the lives of Mālatī and Mādhava, it is a shower of sprays of sandalwood juice (*candanarasacchaṭāsāra*). *Kalita*: Mixed. [10]

[11] *Vyatikara* means intermingling. Today, Fate imitates the union of the life-restoring herb with poison, of brilliance with darkness, and of the thunderbolt with a ray of light. For the thunderbolt is solely of the nature of scorching, while the rays of the moon are solely of the nature of cooling; thus, there is a contradiction between them. [11]

(Behind the scenes) Alas, father! Desist, desist! I am longing for the sight of your lotus-like face. Be gracious; honor me. Why, on my account, do you abandon yourself—who are like a single lamp of auspiciousness for your stainless lineage, which serves as a pillar supporting the space between all the worlds? Furthermore, it was imagined by me, a base woman, that you were devoid of compassion.

The mountain named Lokāloka is a ring-shaped range that encircles all the continents, beyond which the rays of the sun do not spread. Within its interior expanse—that is, its inner width—is a lineage that is stainless and free from blemish; in that lineage, you alone are the auspicious lamp. "Auspicious" (maṅgala) means a form of welfare that is desirable to be wished for; you are its illuminator, meaning its fulfiller. "Merciless" means pitiless.
"It was considered fitting" refers to the intention of having understood the commencement of the gift for the sake of [your] delight.

[Kāmandakī] [12] Just as at the end of the dark fortnight, a single digit of the moon is somehow obtained from another birth, and yet a planet approaches to swallow it—such is this situation of yours. [12] Lavaṅgikā: Alas, dear friend!

[Mādhava] [13] *Pāka* means the yielding of fruit. *Daiva* means previously accumulated karma. *Dvārāṇi* (doors) refers to the means of bringing about the causes of pleasure and pain. *Pidhātum* means to obstruct or ward off. The meaning is: "of that *daiva* which belongs to a living being. [13]

[Mādhava] [14] I have arrived; I have come. (XX) The words beginning with "Having learned of Mālatī’s disappearance" and so forth are the speech of the compassionate forest-dweller. (8) [14] Mādyantikā and Lavangikā: Friend Mālatī! Indeed, I am saying, "Friend Mālatī.
This is merely a form of delirious lamentation. (9)
O Blessed One, protect her! Her heart has long been motionless, its breath having ceased. Alas, Minister! Dear friend! You both have become the cause of each other’s destruction.
"Motionless" means devoid of movement. Regarding "the destruction of each other": having learned of Mālatī’s demise, Bhūrivasu [will die]; anticipating his leap into the fire, Mālatī [will die].

Mādhava will say immediately thereafter that the lightning, rending the mass of clouds, is approaching. And it is by means of the downpour of rain resulting precisely from that rending that the dramatic device for the cessation of everyone's fainting is prepared. True. However, scholars should consider with whom the particle *iva* in the phrase "as if being rent" (*pāṭyamānād iva*) is connected.
(10) [Mādhava] "With a sigh" (*soccvasam*): meaning with the release of sorrow. "Proximity" (*pratyāsatti*): the re-establishment in one's own place of one who has moved away from that place.

[15] *Vitataḥ*: long, which is the expansion of the breath; *unnāhaḥ*: upward movement; *saṃsargaḥ*: connection; by that, *praṇunnau*: impelled, the two breasts in the heart. (11) By the word *tadanu* ("thereafter"), the sequence is also indicated for what precedes. (12) *Prasādi*: clear; it shines forth. By that, it becomes especially radiant. (XX) *Śriyā*: with beauty. *Parigatam*: pervaded on all sides. [15] [OFFSTAGE] [16] *Saṃmadaḥ*: joy. [16]

[Mādhava and Makaranda] [17] *Āsāraḥ*: a downpour of showers; and the shower is of water, and that water is released by the cloud—thus it is a "downpour of the cloud's water. By this, the excellence of its coolness is indicated. For only such a thing is fit to be the means for the natural restoration of life. (XX) [17] Mālatī: By good fortune, I have been restored to life.
Mālatī: How is it that the Blessed Lady is here? (13)
For so long she was unconscious and did not know; but now, having returned to life, she regains her composure.
[Kāmandakī] [18] "To one who is like her own life": to Mādhava. "With frost"—that is, with limbs as cool as the touch of snow.
[18] [Mādhava] "The world of the living": the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
MADAYANTIKĀ and LAVAṄGIKĀ: Dear friend, since you have appeared before us beyond our wildest dreams—meaning, more than we could have imagined—please honor us with an embrace.
*Atirikta*: exceeding; that is to say, beyond the range of perception. *Saṃbhāvaya*: favor; join [us] with it.
Mālatī, overwhelmed by the rising impression of her separation, says:
"O dear friends!
[Kāmandakī] "What is this question regarding them?

[Makaranda and Mādhava] [19] [The answer following the onset of the fruit: "Kapālakuṇḍalā. [20] "A misfortune has occurred": that which has arisen in opposition, consisting of the abduction of Mālatī; by that produced, a calamity—a sudden occurrence in the form of an undesirable contingency; from that, "with difficulty": with hardship, through persistence: by means of incessant exertion. [20] [19]
Lavaṅgikā: (XX) Oh, what a marvel! That the Creator, who is cruel by being repetitive, should be delightful in his final outcome.
Because he repeatedly inflicts suffering, he is "cruel through repetition" (*punaruktadāruṇa*); that which is delightful in the *pariṇāma*—that is, at the conclusion—is truly marvelous.
(XX) [Saudāmanī]: *Antevāsinī* means a close female disciple.

[Kāmandakī] [20]: "Come. By saving the life of Mālatī, you have bestowed life upon many, and through that, you have sustained a great accumulation of merit. "Hanta" expresses joy and wonder. It means that by which delight has been granted. [20]

[21] By the supreme Bodhisattvas: by those who have transcended [the state of being a mere] Buddha. "Formerly" (*purā*): previously, that very acquaintance (*paricaya*) which we had together; that seed, which is conjoined with the desired fruit—that is, characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*)—shines forth (*śālate*) through the abundant fruit that has arisen, attaining a state of praise. (XX) Is it immediately after its own production? No; he says: "by its unfolding" (*vijṛmbhitena*), that is, by its blossoming.

"Unfolding" (*vijṛmbhaṇa*) is the coming together of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) in the form of reaching their respective locations. Even another seed, such as that of a *kalama* rice plant, is not sufficient for its own effect all at once; rather, it [becomes so] through the unfolding of forms such as swelling (*ucchūnatva*), which is acquired through the coming together of earth and other factors.

Regarding the reading "it does not manifest" (*na vijṛmbhate*), the sense is as follows: although there exists a cause that obstructs prior acquaintance—one which incessantly brings forth its own corresponding mass of fruits that are extraordinary to the world—it does not manifest in such a way that prior acquaintance is eclipsed. For the reason is that while a great gain is a cause for egoism in those of fickle minds, it is not so even for the Great-souled ones. (14) [21] MADAYANTIKĀ and LĀVAṄGIKĀ: Is this noble lady Saudāmanī?

Mālatī: Very well. Indeed, by her—who is partial toward our connection with the Holy Lady—I was rebuked by Kapālakuṇḍalā, brought to my own dwelling, and comforted no differently than if it were the Holy Lady herself. Moreover, having arrived here with the *kesarāvalī* (a garland of *vakula* flowers) as a token of recognition in her hand, she has preserved us all.

(15) *Āvasatham*: a house. *Kesarāvalī*: a garland of *vakula* flowers; "that very one" (*sā eva*). "With that as a token of recognition" (*sābhijñānam*): that which produces conviction or proof. "In whose hand" (*haste yasyāḥ*): she who has it thus.
Madayantikā and Lavangikā: The youngest Holy Lady is very gracious toward us.
Saudāmanī is indeed younger than Kāmandakī because, in view of the latter’s status as a preceptor who is the locus of great dignity, she is slightly inferior by virtue of being her disciple.

[Mādhava and Makaranda] [22] "Cintā" (thought) alone is the "pariśrama" (exertion). That which is not thought of bestows [its fruit], while that which is intended for that purpose results in the contradiction of its nature as a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem). Nor has an imitation been made by anyone else. (16) [22] [Saudāmanī] "Hanta! (Ah!). (XX) Nandana’s great joy arises from the union of Makaranda and Madayantī, who are so well-suited to one another.

[Kāmandakī] [23] *Pratyasta* means cast far away; one for whom the calamity consisting of falling to the earth has thus vanished of its own accord is described as such. (XX) *Mahīyasi*: exceeding. *Param*: exceedingly. By that [word]. [B81b] For our joy does not become fruitless. *Preyase*: for the beloved.
[23] Mālatī: By good fortune, the dart of anxiety in my heart has now been removed.

For the uncertainty regarding the union of Makaranda and Madayantikā was like a thorn, because it caused internal anguish. And that has now been removed, since the King has brought about their union and Nandana has welcomed that very purpose.
LAVANGIKĀ: Now, at last, the desires of the illustrious Mādhava and Mālatī have borne fruit without exception.
ALL: Blessed one, you who are the repository of all undertakings, victory to you! O Mādhava, delight of Makaranda, full moon, by good fortune you prosper.

LĀVANGIKĀ: Who indeed, in this great festival where every aspect has been fulfilled, would not be full of jesting? KĀMANDAKĪ: "Variegated" (citram) means possessing various flavors (rasa). "Delightful" (ramaṇīyam) means heart-pleasing. "Radiant" (ujjvalam) means faultless. "Great festival" (mahāprakaraṇam) refers to a grand celebration, for the term *prakaraṇa* is well known to denote a festival in other contexts as well. Furthermore, the poet hints at the transcendent nature of his own composition by employing words with double meanings (*dvyartha*). SAUDĀMANĪ: The connection itself is nectar, because it is difficult to obtain and because it bestows bliss.
Mālatī: How so?
[Makaranda and Mādhava: "The matter occurred otherwise" was said by way of concealment. (XX) Synonym for *vacana* is *krama*; that—namely "otherwise"—is inconsistent with the concealment.
(XX) Lavaṅgikā: Venerable lady, what should be done?
The truth of the matter has become manifest. What is to be done here? The sense is: "Is that reason for which it was previously concealed no longer present now?
[Kāmandakī] "In the same way" means *janāntika* (aside).

(XX) "From favor": from compliance. "The state of being a disciple": the stage of listening to the scriptures. "Of us": of ourselves and of Saudāmanī. "The primary constituent" (*pradhānaprakṛti*) is the king. The constituents (*prakṛtis*) are the sovereign, the minister, the territory, the fort, the treasury, the army, and the ally.

[Mādhava and Makaranda: "Possessing unimpeded majesty": they are fully capable of accomplishing their own purposes without restraint. [Kāmandakī: "[By our] desires" refers to those of Bhūrivasu and Devarāta. "[Of the two] long-lived ones" refers to yourself and Mālatī. "Auspiciousness" means in the form of their marriage. "By means of efforts": by means of activities. "Of my two disciples": of Avalokitā and Buddharakṣitā; even that suffering has borne fruit. "Expert": one whose future outcome is skillful. "Of your beloved": of Makaranda. "Beloved" (preyas): more dear. [24]

[Mādhava: [25] “May they be peaceful. With the first quarter-verse, he offers auspicious blessings to the Brāhmaṇas; with the second, to the Kṣatriyas; with the third, to the Vaiśyas; and with the fourth, to the Śūdras. “In a dense assembly of kinsmen, relatives, and friends”: those who possess such joy (*pramoda*) are so described. (XX) “May they rejoice” indicates drinking together, eating together, and so forth. The word “dense” (*ghana*) implies being closely gathered. “Kinsmen and relatives” is an expression used in common worldly parlance. “Assembly” (*goṣṭhī*) means a gathering or council. (XX) [25] “May it be auspicious! (*Bhadram*).

Thus ends the tenth act in this commentary on the drama *Mālatīmādhava*, composed by the illustrious Hariharamiśra, son of the illustrious Amoghadeva. The venerable Hariharamiśra, a member of the Parāśara lineage, has composed this concise and elegant commentary in order to provide understanding for this difficult work.
In the year [of the cycle] known as Ṣaḍvahnirāma (1366), on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa,
under the yoga Amṛta and when Jupiter was in the sign of Virgo, during the reign of King Arimalla Deva.
